lesson.title: Surviving the Winter: The Continental Army at Valley Forge
lesson.summary: During the harsh winter of 1777 to 1778, Washington's Continental Army nearly fell apart from cold, hunger, and disease at Valley Forge, but emerged as a more disciplined fighting force.
lesson.body:
After a difficult 1777 campaign that included the loss of Philadelphia to British forces, George Washington marched his Continental Army to Valley Forge, Pennsylvania, about twenty miles northwest of the captured capital, to make winter camp where it could watch the British without risking an open battle in poor weather. The army settled in at Valley Forge in December 1777 and remained there until June 1778, a stretch of roughly six months that became one of the most severe tests the Revolutionary cause faced anywhere in the war.

Conditions at the camp were brutal. Roughly twelve thousand soldiers, along with a number of camp followers including soldiers' wives and children, crowded into hastily built log huts with inadequate clothing, blankets, and food. Supply shortages, worsened by a weak and disorganized Continental supply system and by local farmers who sometimes found it more profitable to sell food to the British in occupied Philadelphia than to Washington's underfunded army, left many soldiers without shoes even as they marched through snow. Disease spread rapidly through the crowded, unsanitary camp, and by the time spring arrived, an estimated two thousand soldiers, something close to one in six of those present, had died from sickness, exposure, or malnutrition rather than combat.

Despite these hardships, Valley Forge became a turning point in the army's development rather than simply a story of suffering. In February 1778, a Prussian born military officer, Baron Friedrich Wilhelm von Steuben, arrived at camp and, though he spoke little English and relied on translators and profanity in multiple languages to make himself understood, began drilling the Continental Army in European style discipline, marching formations, sanitation, and the effective use of the bayonet. Steuben's training methods, later written up in a manual that became the army's standard drill book for years afterward, transformed a collection of often ragged militia companies into a more cohesive, professional fighting force.

News that reached camp in the spring of 1778 gave the exhausted army a further boost. France, persuaded in part by the American victory at Saratoga the previous fall, formally allied with the United States in a treaty signed in February 1778, promising money, soldiers, and naval power that would prove decisive in the war's final years. Martha Washington also visited the camp that winter, helping organize aid for sick and wounded soldiers alongside her husband's staff.

When the army marched out of Valley Forge in June 1778, it was smaller than when it had arrived, but it was also better trained, better organized, and reinforced by the promise of French support. The army that emerged from that terrible winter went on to fight British forces to a draw at the Battle of Monmouth later that same month, an early sign that the discipline learned at Valley Forge was already paying off on the battlefield.
